title: Meerut 'Blue Drum' Murder: Muskan and Sahil Sentenced to Death
excerpt: A Meerut court handed down the death penalty after a 13-month trial built on circumstantial evidence, 126 hearings and 22 witnesses in the killing of merchant navy officer Saurabh Rajput.
body:
• A Meerut district court on Wednesday sentenced Muskan Rastogi and Sahil Shukla to death for the March 2025 murder of merchant navy officer Saurabh Rajput.
  • The pair were convicted on September 30 of murder and concealing the body, which was found dismembered inside a blue plastic drum sealed with cement.
  • The trial ran about 13 months across 126 hearings, with 22 prosecution witnesses and no eyewitness — the case rested on circumstantial, technical and physical evidence.
  • A district court death sentence in India must still be confirmed by the High Court before it can be carried out.

A district court in Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, on Wednesday sentenced Muskan Rastogi and her partner Sahil Shukla to death for killing her husband, Saurabh Rajput, in the case that became known across India as the 'blue drum' murder. District Judge Arvind Kumar Mishra pronounced the sentence, with both convicts appearing by video conference, according to court officials reported by Aaj Tak and The English Post.

The court had convicted both on September 30 of murder and of concealing Rajput's body. Reports of the sentencing also said fines were imposed alongside the death penalty. In remarks reported from the courtroom, the judge invoked the idea that punishment itself is a duty — a point lawyers summarised to reporters after the hearing.

How the crime came to light

According to the police investigation, Rajput, a merchant navy officer, had returned to Meerut from London in late February 2025. Prosecutors said that on March 3, 2025, he was sedated at home, killed, and his body was then dismembered. The remains were placed in a large blue plastic drum, which was filled with a mixture of sand, water and cement and sealed.

The case surfaced later that month, and the remains were recovered from the drum at the Meerut home on March 17, 2025. The method of concealment drew nationwide attention and gave the case its name. After the killing, the pair travelled to Himachal Pradesh, according to evidence presented in court, before they were arrested.

A case built without an eyewitness

There was no eyewitness to the killing. The prosecution instead built a chain of circumstantial evidence and presented it in sequence. Prosecutor Vijay Bahadur said after the conviction that the court had found the evidence complete and that all the testimonies corroborated the prosecution's case.

"We had presented 22 testimonies on different occasions. The case was based on circumstantial evidence."

— Vijay Bahadur, Prosecutor

Those witnesses included shopkeepers who, according to the prosecution, sold the drum, cement, sand and blades before the murder, as well as hotel managers and cab drivers. Call records and mobile tower locations were used to place Shukla at the house at the time of the crime and to trace the pair's movements afterwards. The trial moved to the district judge's court in July 2025 and continued for about 13 months.

The defence argued that nobody had directly seen the murder and asked the court to consider that both accused have daughters. The court set those submissions aside and imposed the maximum punishment, lawyers told reporters.

What happens next

The sentence does not end the legal process. A death sentence passed by a district court must be confirmed by the High Court, and the convicts can appeal. Rajput's family, who said they had fought the case for about a year and a half, welcomed the verdict. His mother had publicly demanded the death penalty, and his brother said the family's only demand was justice.

For now, the judgment closes the trial phase of one of India's most closely followed murder cases of 2025 — a case decided not on a single witness, but on purchases, phone records and 22 corroborating accounts pieced together over 126 hearings.
